summary: Marrowstone Point Light, Jefferson County, Washington: a red post lantern from 1888, a clockwork fog bell in 1896, a concrete fog-signal building in 1918, automated in 1962.

lens.note: 250 mm optic on a mast on the fog-signal building (HistoryLink)

structures.note: Red light about 15 ft high on a pole, tended by a contract keeper (HistoryLink; LighthouseFriends)
One-and-a-half-story (LighthouseFriends, quoting the notice to mariners) or large two-story (HistoryLink); USLHS gives 1895
20 ft high; the light stands on its roof at 28 ft (HistoryLink)

access.note: Not open to the public; the light can be seen from the beach at Fort Flagler State Park (HistoryLink, 2004). The USLHS page says 'Open to Public: Yes'.

visit.note: Field station grounds are not open to the public (HistoryLink).

facts.agency: U.S. Coast Guard maintains the light (Aids to Navigation Branch, Seattle); the field station grounds are USGS-run (HistoryLink)

corrections.proposed: post lantern, built 1888, about 4.6 m (15 ft), replaced; square concrete fog-signal building with the light on its roof, built 1918, about 6.1 m, with the optic 8.5 m above base
corrections.why: The 1888 mark was a post lantern on a pole, not a tower (HistoryLink; LighthouseFriends). The 8.5 m figure is the optic's height on the 1918 fog-signal building (HistoryLink: 28 ft).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: 1888 is the year of the first light, a red post lantern (HistoryLink; LighthouseFriends). The 1912 (Wikidata) and 1914 (USLHS tower year) dates refer to a later concrete structure; HistoryLink dates the present light building to 1918. The story gives 1888 for the first light and 1918 for the present building, and names the disagreement on the rest.

The light is an active aid (LighthouseFriends: a flashing white light is exhibited from the 1917 structure; HistoryLink: the Coast Guard maintains it). The USLHS field 'Active Aid to Navigation? No' is not supported by either essay and is recorded here as a disagreement.
The story follows HistoryLink (the station is not open to the public, the light is visible from the beach). The USLHS field says 'Open to Public: Yes' and gives no date.

notes_for_editor: Disagreements the story shows rather than settles: (1) first concrete light: 1912 (Wikipedia lead, not cited), 1914 (LighthouseFriends; USLHS tower year), 1918 (HistoryLink); (2) fog gun 1913 (HistoryLink) vs 1 April 1914 (LighthouseFriends; Bulletin 1914); (3) Daboll 17 Dec 1917 (LighthouseFriends) vs 1918 (HistoryLink) vs 'reed horn' (Commissioner 1919; Bulletin 1918); (4) keeper's dwelling 1895 (USLHS) vs 1896 (LighthouseFriends, HistoryLink); one-and-a-half-story (LighthouseFriends) vs two-story (HistoryLink); (5) North Pacific: 'only fourteen passengers' (SF Call, 20 July 1903) vs 40 passengers and crew (HistoryLink, which dates the sinking to 2 a.m. 19 July); (6) Rustad's sons: three (HistoryLink) vs four (LighthouseFriends); (7) 1972 vs 1974 ownership changes; (8) range: 'visible for nine miles' (HistoryLink) vs record 7 nm; (9) characteristic: record Fl W 6s (OSM) and Oc W 6s (Wikidata) vs HistoryLink's 'fixed white light occulting every four seconds' and LighthouseFriends' 'flashing white'; not resolved; (10) ownership: Washington State Parks (Salish Sea Lighthouses) vs federal field station (HistoryLink); (11) USLHS 'Active Aid to Navigation? No' vs active elsewhere; (12) USLHS 'Open to Public: Yes' vs HistoryLink's closed. Name variant: USLHS 'Osmore H. Morgan', HistoryLink 'Osmond Hale Morgan'; the roster name is used in the story. Corpus check: the 1893-1897 Light-House Board entries were read at scan pages; printed page numbers were not confirmed for them, so the footnotes cite scan pages. The 1917-1919 Commissioner entries carry printed pages only where the scan data confirmed them (1917 printed p. 52, 1919 printed p. 50). The 1880 Life-Saving Service tables that name 'Marrowstone Point, Wash. Ter.' list stranded vessels, not this light, and are not used. The Wikipedia article was read for leads only and is not cited. The 1912 Wikidata first-lit year and the 1888 'tower' structure in the record are the two main record errors (see corrections). No photographs were added: HistoryLink and LighthouseFriends carry photographs from the USCG, NARA, USGS and the Puget Sound Maritime Historical Society whose licences were not checked. Fact-check 2026-10-28 additions: (a) the 1918 Commissioner report (scan p.360) also records a change in the fog signal 'from acetylene gun to third-class Daboll trumpet', so the Daboll is named in both 1918 and 1917-18 sources while the 1919 report and the 1918 Bulletin say reed horn; the story states both. (b) The 1896 Light-House Board page (scan p.201) was confirmed by archive.org in-item search (corpus.py page --api), not by the local page index, which has none for that volume. (c) LighthouseFriends says the station is owned by the US Geological Survey and that the shoreline is open; both are now in the story. (d) LighthouseFriends' 'flashing white' and HistoryLink's 'fixed white light occulting every four seconds' are both stated. (e) The SF Call of 20 July 1903 says 'this morning' for the wreck; the story dates it to 19 July from HistoryLink's 2 a.m. time and footnotes both. (f) Name variant: HistoryLink 'Annette "Nettie" (Morgan) Race'; the story uses Nettie, as the USLHS roster and LighthouseFriends do. (g) The 1880 Life-Saving Service tables that name Marrowstone Point are not used, and the story no longer calls the 1892 collision the earliest wreck the sources record, only the earliest in these sources. The Wikipedia lead was not cited.
